Drill: Customer Segmentation

Cross-cutting drill · The course’s only end-to-end unsupervised exercise: scale + one-hot a mixed customer table, choose the cluster count by elbow (WCSS) and silhouette, run K-Means, visualize the result in 2D with PCA, then interpret the segments against a held-aside label.

What this exercise teaches

The full unsupervised-segmentation pipeline: preprocess mixed numeric/categorical data, pick k without labels via elbow + silhouette, cluster with K-Means, project to 2D with PCA for a sanity-check picture, and interpret each cluster by its feature profile and subscription rate. It is the only exercise where there is no target to train against — y is set aside and used only afterwards to make sense of the clusters.

Dataset not available locally [DATA-2]. The solution loads the UCI Bank Marketing file bank-additional-full.csv (41,188 rows, 20 inputs) from ../../data/bank_marketing_data_set/bank-additional/bank-additional-full.csv. That file is not present in this repo’s data/ folder (only Titanic, house-prices, and seeds are), and the VHL notebook export has no saved cell outputs. So this page documents the idioms and decisions from the notebook but does not reproduce any numbers — no shapes, WCSS, silhouette values, or cluster stats are quoted, because none exist to cite and none will be fabricated. To run it yourself, download the dataset from https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/datasets/Bank+Marketing and fix the path. For worked, runnable K-Means and PCA examples on present data, use the method pages linked below (their examples use Iris / seeds / Wholesale Customers).

Setup

  • Dataset (intended): UCI Bank Marketing — Portuguese bank direct-marketing campaigns. The full variant bank-additional-full.csv has 41,188 rows and 20 input columns; the CSV uses a semicolon separator and the literal string 'unknown' for missing values.
  • Loader (VHL cell 2): pd.read_csv('../../data/bank_marketing_data_set/bank-additional/bank-additional-full.csv', sep=';').
  • Numeric columns (exact, VHL cell 6): age, duration, campaign, pdays, previous, emp.var.rate, cons.price.idx, cons.conf.idx, euribor3m, nr.employed. All other columns (job, marital, education, default, housing, loan, contact, month, day_of_week, poutcome) are categorical.
  • Target (held aside, not used for clustering): y — binary yes/no, whether the client subscribed to a term deposit.
  • Task: load + preprocess → visualize → K-Means with elbow/silhouette → PCA 2D plot → interpret clusters.
  • Expected output: preprocessed feature shape; numeric histograms + a correlation heatmap; WCSS and silhouette per k (2–10); a chosen k (the notebook picks 3) with labels; a PCA scatter coloured by cluster; per-cluster numeric summaries and target distributions. (All unsaved in this export — see the callout above.)

Walkthrough

Step 1 — load and clean missing values (VHL cells 2, 4). Two decisions are easy to miss: the sep=';' and treating 'unknown' as missing before dropping:

df = pd.read_csv('.../bank-additional-full.csv', sep=';')
df.replace('unknown', np.nan, inplace=True)
df.dropna(inplace=True)                  # drops every row with any 'unknown'

Step 2 — scale numerics, one-hot categoricals, drop the label (VHL cell 6). The target is separated first; numerics are standardized; categoricals are one-hot encoded with drop_first=True:

target = df['y']
df_features = df.drop('y', axis=1)
categorical_cols = [c for c in df_features.columns if c not in numeric_cols]
df_features[numeric_cols] = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df_features[numeric_cols])
X = pd.get_dummies(df_features, columns=categorical_cols, drop_first=True)

The decisive idea: K-Means uses Euclidean distance, so features must be on comparable scales — hence StandardScaler on the numerics — and categoricals must become numbers, hence get_dummies. Dropping y is mandatory: clustering is unsupervised.

Step 3 — pick k by elbow + silhouette, then cluster (VHL cell 10). Sweep k from 2 to 10, collecting inertia (WCSS) and silhouette for each, then commit to a chosen k:

for k in range(2, 11):
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
    kmeans.fit(X)
    wcss.append(kmeans.inertia_)                       # within-cluster sum of squares
    silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_score(X, kmeans.labels_))
# ...inspect the two curves...
optimal_k = 3
cluster_labels = KMeans(n_clusters=optimal_k, random_state=42).fit_predict(X)

Choosing k=3 is a judgment call read off the elbow and silhouette plots — not an automatic result. See K-Means for how to read both diagnostics.

Step 4 — PCA to 2D for visualization (VHL cell 12). PCA here is purely for plotting the high-dimensional clusters, not for modelling:

X_pca = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=42).fit_transform(X)
sns.scatterplot(x=X_pca[:, 0], y=X_pca[:, 1], hue=cluster_labels, palette='Set1', s=50)

Some overlap in 2D is expected — two components rarely capture all the structure of a wide one-hot feature space. See PCA.

Step 5 — interpret clusters against the held-aside y (VHL cell 14). Re-attach the labels and profile each cluster, including its subscription rate:

df['cluster'] = cluster_labels
for c in range(optimal_k):
    display(df[df['cluster'] == c][numeric_cols].describe())
    print(df[df['cluster'] == c]['y'].value_counts())   # which segments subscribe

This is where y finally enters — as a post-hoc interpretation aid, asking which segment is most likely to subscribe, never as a clustering input.

The traps that bite in unsupervised work.

  • Wrong separator or unhandled 'unknown'. Forget sep=';' and the file loads as one column; forget the 'unknown'→NaN step and “missing” values silently survive.
  • dropna() can shrink the data a lot. Many columns use 'unknown', so dropping every affected row removes a sizeable fraction — note how much you lose.
  • duration leaks the outcome. The UCI data description warns duration (call length) is known only after the call and essentially determines y. Including it in clustering is questionable for honest segmentation; consider dropping it.
  • One-hot blows up the dimensionality and mixes geometries — Euclidean distance over 0/1 dummies behaves very differently from distance over standardized continuous features. K-Means treats them all alike, which is a real limitation here.
  • K-Means depends on initialization. With random_state=42 and default n_init, results are reproducible but the elbow at k=3 is still a judgment, not a fact.

Common pitfalls

The conceptual one underneath all of the above: clustering finds structure in the features you give it, so preprocessing is the model. Scaling, encoding, and which columns you include (especially the leaky duration) change the clusters more than any K-Means setting. And because there is no ground truth during fitting, you cannot “score” the result — you justify k with elbow + silhouette and validate the segments by whether they tell a coherent story (their feature profiles and, here, their subscription rates).

What this exercise teaches that the others don’t

It is the only unsupervised-learning exercise: K-Means, cluster-count selection by elbow (WCSS) + silhouette, and PCA for visualizing high-dimensional clusters. It is the only one combining one-hot encoding of many categoricals with scaled numerics for distance-based modelling, and the only one interpreting clusters against a held-aside label rather than predicting it. Every other drill has a target to optimize; here the work is finding and explaining structure with none.

Supervised learning asks “predict y”; this asks “what natural groups exist?” — so there is no accuracy to chase. The deliverables are a defensible k (elbow + silhouette), a 2D PCA picture that shows the groups are real, and a plain-language profile of each segment. The course’s lecture K-Means/PCA examples use present datasets (Iris, seeds, Wholesale Customers); pair this drill with those for runnable practice.
